lines.text: Port Fennick is getting every pothole fixed at once, and Mayor Bunbury picked the week himself: right before his election.
It sleeps under a tarp eleven months a year, then spends two frantic weeks paving anything that holds still.
He's even dusted off his speech: same as last time, new date.
Well, potholes don't vote, but the people who hit them do.
Fix a road in March, and nobody remembers by November. Fix it the week they vote, and he's a local hero.
Economists even have a name for it: the political budget cycle.
Election day in Port Fennick: November fifth.
One meeting with Gus at Smoothly Paving, and every crew is booked for late October. His only question: overtime?
And his campaign slogan practically writes itself: re-elect me, or keep the potholes.
And you? You get the other eleven months.
Your bike finds one on Monday, your car finds two on Tuesday, and by Friday the big one has its own mailbox.
Then, two weeks before the vote, the tarp comes off,
and weekly repairs leap from zero to four hundred, just in time for the ballot box.
Bunbury cruises to a fifth term.
Ask what comes next, and he swears the roads are in safe hands.
Then the tarp goes back on, and the crews go back on holiday.
As for the pothole outside your door? Re-elected, for four more years.
